up.note: A classical algorithm is a quantum one, so the only content is the change of cost convention. $\mathrm{R}_0$ is worst-case expected cost (worst-case cost would collapse to $\mathrm{D}$); $\mathrm{Q}_0$ charges the worst case and pays for it with the $\bot$ outcome. Truncate the Las Vegas algorithm after $2\,\mathrm{R}_0(f)$ queries and output $\bot$ if it has not finished: by Markov it finishes with probability $\ge 1/2$, and when it finishes it is right. The same truncation works for partial functions and relations, and in the other direction repeating a $\bot$-algorithm until it answers costs $2\,\mathrm{Q}_0$ in expectation -- the two conventions agree up to a factor of two.

    A classical algorithm is a quantum one, so the only content is the change of cost convention. $\mathrm{R}_0$ is worst-case expected cost (worst-case cost would collapse to $\mathrm{D}$); $\mathrm{Q}_0$ charges the worst case and pays for it with the $\bot$ outcome. Truncate the Las Vegas algorithm after $2\,\mathrm{R}_0(f)$ queries and output $\bot$ if it has not finished: by Markov it finishes with probability $\ge 1/2$, and when it finishes it is right. The same truncation works for partial functions and relations, and in the other direction repeating a $\bot$-algorithm until it answers costs $2\,\mathrm{Q}_0$ in expectation -- the two conventions agree up to a factor of two.

Recording this edge is what keeps the $\mathrm{Q}_0$ column honest: without it nothing stops a $\mathrm{Q}_0$ value from being entered above the function's own $\mathrm{R}_0$. Note also that the polynomial floor under $\mathrm{Q}_0$ is $\mathrm{rdeg}/2$, not $\deg/2$ -- see the $\mathrm{Q}_0$ measure page.

facts: The polynomial floor under $\mathrm{Q}_0$ is $\mathrm{rdeg}/2$, not $\deg/2$. Writing $p_b$ for the probability of output $b$ after $T$ queries -- a polynomial of degree $\le 2T$ -- zero error says only that $p_1$ vanishes on $f^{-1}(0)$ and $p_0$ vanishes on $f^{-1}(1)$. So $p_1$ is a nondeterministic polynomial for $f$ and $p_0$ one for $\bar f$, giving $\mathrm{Q}_0(f) \ge \tfrac12\max\{\mathrm{ndeg}(f), \mathrm{ndeg}(\bar f)\} = \mathrm{rdeg}(f)/2 \ge \mathrm{NQ}(f) - \tfrac12$ -- a zero-error algorithm is in particular a nondeterministic one for $f$ and for $\bar f$. The stronger $\deg(f) \le 2T$ needs $p_1 = f$ exactly, which is $\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{E}}$; the difference is real, and it is large -- on \(\bar{\wedge}\text{-tree}\) $\deg = N$ while $\mathrm{rdeg} = \Theta(\sqrt N)$.
For total $f$, $\mathrm{Q}_0$ is polynomially related to all the other measures; the exact relations to $\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{E}}$ are less studied than the $\mathrm{R}_0$-vs-$\mathrm{R}$ ones.

New certification lower bounds: $\mathrm{Q}_{\mathrm{E}}^{\mathrm{cert}}=\Theta(\mathrm{Q}_0^{\mathrm{cert}})=O(\mathrm{Q}_0)$, $\overline{\deg}^{\mathrm{cert}}=O(\mathrm{Q}_0)$, and $\overline{\mathrm{osdeg}}=O(\mathrm{Q}_0)$ [KLLPV26].

AND of complemented EXACT-ONE functions has $\mathrm{Q}_0=\widetilde\Theta(m^{3/2})$ but $\mathrm{Q}=\Theta(m)$ and $\mathrm{rdeg}=m$; bounded degree certification proves the stronger lower bound [KLLPV26, Theorem 10 and Lemma 55].
self.name: Zero-error (Las Vegas) quantum query complexity
self.short: Quantum algorithm that never errs but may output "don't know" with probability <= 1/2.
